query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Hf with Al in as-cast HfMoTaTiZr will reduce density by ≥5% while preserving its ~1600 MPa room-temperature yield strength and ~850 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr (single-phase BCC) with density ≈10.21 g/cm³, yield strength ≈1600 MPa at 25 °C and ≈855 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Replace a small fraction (5–10 at%) of Hf with Al in the alloy during vacuum arc melting, followed by standard homogenization heat treatment.
generation.conditions: Compression or tensile testing at 25 °C and 1000 °C in an inert or ambient atmosphere, maintaining a nominal strain rate (e.g., 10−3 s−1).
generation.structural_mediator: Solid-solution strengthening and lattice distortion due to Al substitution for heavier Hf, retaining a predominantly BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Introducing Al decreases overall atomic mass and induces localized lattice strains, which can preserve or slightly enhance strength through solid-solution strengthening while reducing density.
generation.predicted_outcome: Density drops by ≥5% relative to 10.21 g/cm³, with yield strengths at 25 °C and 1000 °C remaining within ±5% of the baseline values, preserving the strong performance of the parent alloy.
generation.baseline: Unmodified HfMoTaTiZr: density ~10.21 g/cm³, yield strength ~1600 MPa (25 °C), ~855 MPa (1000 °C).
generation.boundary: Excess Al (>10 at%) may lead to detrimental secondary phases or significantly reduced ductility.
generation.uncertainty: Local variation in microstructure or formation of secondary phases could diminish high-temperature performance or fracture toughness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Hf(1−x)Al(x)MoTaTiZr alloys at x=0.05 and x=0.10 by arc melting, homogenize, and machine test specimens for mechanical tests at 25 °C and 1000 °C alongside baseline HfMoTaTiZr.
measurements: Yield strength in compression or tension at 25 °C
Yield strength in compression or tension at 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy’s density is not reduced by at least 5% or if yield strengths at 25 °C or 1000 °C drop more than 5% below baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Xu et al. [] reduced the density of the Ti50-xAlxV20Nb20Mo10 RHEA from 6.102 g/cm3 (Ti40Al10V20Nb20Mo10) to 5.876 g/cm3 (Ti30Al20V20Nb20Mo10) by adjusting the Al content, and the room-temperature specific yield strength increased from 147.49 MPa*cm3/g to 202.01 MPa*cm3/g. Although the density and specific strength of these alloys are significantly improved after the addition of aluminum, their plasticity is generally reduced. Therefore, choosing a refractory high-entropy alloy with both high strength and high plasticity as a matrix, and then reducing its density by adding light elements such as Al, is an effective method to obtain structural materials with high strength, low density, and good plasticity. The recently reported TaNbVTi alloy meets the requirements of the matrix very well []. Furthermore, Yang et al. [] reported that the arc-melted NbTiVTaAl0.25 HEA has a low density of 8.78 g/cm3 and reasonable plasticity greater than 50%. Nevertheless, the yield strength of this alloy is only 1330 MPa (specific strength of 151.48 MPa*cm3/g), which has the possibility of further improvement compared with most refractory high-entropy alloys.
